extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific inquiry (scientists, physicians, social scientists, philosophers of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for choosing, conducting, and judging methods of investigation (deductive, empirical, observational, experimental) when inferring causal laws, especially for complex phenomena in medicine, physiology, and social/political science.

rubrics_metrics.name: State laws of causation as tendencies, not actual results
rubrics_metrics.description: All laws of causation, in consequence of their liability to be counteracted, require to be stated in words affirmative of tendencies only, and not of actual results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use language that expresses a tendency (e.g., 'tend to fall', 'pressure' as tendency to motion) rather than asserting absolute outcomes; this avoids the misconception that general laws have exceptions and clarifies that apparent exceptions are often other concurrent tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize concurrent causes and disturbing forces (do not call them exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: What is thought to be an exception to a principle is usually some other and distinct principle cutting into the former; some other force which impinges against the first force, and deflects it from its direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat multiple active causes as concurrent laws rather than framing one as a rule and the other as an exception; explain supposed exceptions (e.g., balloon not falling) as the action of other real tendencies (atmospheric resistance) that modify but do not negate the original tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer deductive (a priori) method for complex, multi-cause phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of an effect compounded of many causes is a result of the laws of the separate causes on the combination of which it depends; this is called the method a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deduction when direct observation/experiment on the complex effect is impractical due to plurality of causes; requires prior knowledge (by induction or prior deduction) of the laws of the separate causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish observation vs experiment within a posteriori methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The a posteriori method subdivides: (1) collating instances of the effect (pure observation / Method of Agreement), and (2) operating upon the causes and trying different combinations (experiment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit which variety is being used and aware of their differing strengths and limits when inferring causal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying solely on pure observation for multifactorial effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple observation (Method of Agreement) is inapplicable to ascertain conditions of effects dependent on many concurring causes; such observation yields at best vague impressions rather than useful conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generalize from observed coincidences in complex cases (e.g., whether mercury cures a disease) because many other causes can produce the same effect, so recoveries will not consistently correlate with the agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental precautions: ascertain and control all relevant circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: When we devise an experiment to ascertain the effect of a given agent, we introduce the agent into the midst of a set of circumstances which we have exactly ascertained; and we require that none of the known circumstances shall have effects confounded with those of the agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select well-ascertained circumstances, exclude or account for other causes capable of composition with the given cause, and if any are present make them such that their influence can be computed and allowed for; this is often infeasible in life sciences and social contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: When empirically testing complex cases, avoid importing deductive premises
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimental method, to be truly empirical, must make entire abstraction of all knowledge of the simpler tendencies, and aim at obtaining a direct answer to the specific question (e.g., does mercury tend to cure?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If experiments use prior deductions about component causes, they become deductive rather than purely empirical tests; be clear about which approach is being undertaken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Method of Concomitant Variations cautiously (it is useful but encumbered)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Concomitant Variations can help where causes cannot be wholly separated, but it is encumbered by the peculiar difficulties of complex subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this method where appropriate, but recognize its limits in the presence of many interacting, changing influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite for deduction: ascertain laws of separate causes (preferably in isolation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the law of an effect from the laws of the different tendencies which produce it, the first requisite is to know the laws of those tendencies, which supposes previous observation/experiment on each cause separately or a prior deduction from other observed laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study each cause in cases where it operates alone or only with agencies whose effects can be calculated and allowed for; avoid using instances where the tendency is counteracted as the inductive basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction is foundational to deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step in the Deductive Method is an inductive operation because there must be a direct induction as the basis of the whole, though that induction may sometimes be supplied by a prior deduction whose premises ultimately rest on induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that the premises used in deduction have been grounded in observation or experiment, directly or indirectly; do not treat deduction as free from empirical foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive method comprises three essential operations: induction, ratiocination, verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deductive Method consists of (1) an inductive operation to learn laws of causes, (2) ratiocination to determine effects from those laws, and (3) verification by comparison with observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three stages are necessary: without verification, deductive results remain conjectural; without induction, the premises are unsupported; without ratiocination, premises cannot yield particular predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratiocination: reason from known laws to predict or infer causes
rubrics_metrics.description: This is a process of calculation (in a wide sense) to determine, given laws of causes, what effect a certain combination will produce or what combination would produce a given effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May require advanced mathematics or geometry where quantitative laws exist; often infeasible for highly complex systems, and then only approximate reasoning is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification: test deductions against direct observation wherever possible
rubrics_metrics.description: To warrant reliance on general conclusions arrived at by deduction, these conclusions must be found, on careful comparison, to accord with the results of direct observation wherever it can be had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If observations confirm deductions, they can be trusted elsewhere; if they do not, one must account for the discrepancy (show what frustrated the expected effect) or regard the theory as imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not induce laws from instances where the tendency is counteracted or modified
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot expect to find the law of a tendency by an induction from cases in which the tendency is counteracted (e.g., laws of motion could not be found from observing bodies kept at rest by equilibrium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek instances in which the tendency operates unconfounded, or where interfering agencies are known and can be allowed for, to derive reliable inductive laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: In physiology/medicine prefer pathological facts and experiments in health for inductive insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathological facts often afford the most valuable equivalent to experimentation in physiology because they can exhibit a definite disturbance in some organ while others remain (initially) unaffected; experiments are best tried in the condition of health rather than disease when seeking general laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe early stages of derangement to trace causal chains, use artificial pathological experiments (e.g., nerve section) for discovering functions, and prefer controlled trials in health to reveal basic laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiply experiments to attenuate unknown causes, but recognize limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulties from unknown circumstances may be attenuated by sufficient multiplication of experiments in circumstances making it improbable that the unknown causes exist in them all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated trials across varied contexts to reduce chance that an unknown confounder explains the result, but be cautious because in many complex cases this may still be inadequate to establish causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental/inductive reasoning is especially weak for political and historical phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Plurality of Causes is excessive in politics and history and the effects are interwoven; collating individual instances or attempting experiments will rarely yield reliable induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of attempts to infer causal rules for large-scale social results purely from collation of instances or pseudo-experimental comparisons (e.g., 'country prospered under institution X'); recognize that changing background conditions vitiate such comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer precise nomenclature to avoid superficial categorizations
rubrics_metrics.description: To call one of concurrent principles an exception to another is superficial and contrary to correct principles of nomenclature and arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify effects arising from the same kind and cause under the same category, rather than splitting them artificially based on dominance of one cause in particular cases; improve terminology where a more accurate term (e.g., 'pressure' for tendency to motion) clarifies the causal relation.
